strengths: The paper offers a useful Algorithms/General contribution to GUI grounding: it supervises intrinsic multimodal attention through an anchor token, with instruction-dependent head weighting and overlap-aware patch labels. Using existing attention rather than an additional grounding module is a coherent and practically relevant design.

Results across three benchmarks support the method’s effectiveness. Without zoom-in, GUI-AIMA achieves 45.2% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 56.9% on OSWorld-G, versus 42.2% and 54.6% for GUI-Actor-3B. Two-pass inference raises these results to 58.6% and 62.2%. ScreenSpot-v2 performance remains competitive at 90.8%.

The controlled 45k-example ablation is particularly valuable. On ScreenSpot-Pro, anchor-based uniform aggregation improves over vanilla attention grounding from 37.51% to 40.23%; global token-based weighting reaches 42.13%; weighted labels further improve this to 43.39%. These comparisons provide evidence beyond heterogeneous published benchmark results.

The zoom-in analysis reports both recovered and newly incorrect predictions, providing a useful account of the refinement tradeoff. Training sources and major optimization settings are identified, and the method explicitly acknowledges its relationship to TAG, GUI-Actor, and Gaussian grounding supervision.
weaknesses: The strongest headline improvements combine the proposed model with additional inference computation. Comparable crop-and-zoom evaluation is not provided for GUI-Actor or coordinate-generating baselines, although this refinement is not exclusive to attention-based grounding. Consequently, the results establish a strong overall system more clearly than a uniquely superior grounding formulation.

Efficiency claims exceed the measurements. Figure 4 compares convergence against training steps, without wall-clock time, memory consumption, or inference latency. Extracting attention and hidden states across layers can introduce substantial overhead. Likewise, 85k screenshots correspond to 259k instruction examples; a controlled data-scaling comparison is needed to establish superior sample efficiency rather than simply good performance with this dataset.

The explanation that visual-sink selection identifies semantic heads and preserves general capabilities remains weakly substantiated. All parameters are unfrozen, and no general-capability retention evaluation is reported. Appendix A provides only a few token-correlation examples; its claim about the end-of-message token is also misleading, since that token does not have the largest embedding-based correlation in the displayed examples. The ablations support the weighting heuristic, but not the full mechanistic interpretation.

Several implementation details impede reproduction. The manuscript does not clearly specify the attention-map-to-click rule, input resolution/token budget, or relative weighting of attention and next-token losses. Equation (11) gives negative KL divergence as a head weight without explicitly applying the nonnegative normalization required for aggregation; constructing a probability distribution from potentially negative cosine similarities also needs clarification. These may be reporting omissions, but they affect the soft variant’s mathematical specification.

The evaluation protocol needs clarification. Table 5 starts from 47.06%, apparently the soft variant, while Table 1 labels the zoom-in result as ordinary GUI-AIMA. The manuscript also does not identify a separate validation set for selecting head-weighting and zoom parameters, and small gains such as 90.8% versus 90.4% on ScreenSpot-v2 lack uncertainty estimates. These concerns temper confidence in the broad superiority claims, although the larger controlled ablation gains still support a borderline acceptance.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution, GUI-AIMA offers a useful refinement of coordinate-free GUI grounding: supervising intrinsic attention through an anchor token, with instruction-dependent head weighting and overlap-aware patch labels. The distinction from TAG and GUI-Actor is reasonably clear, and the method avoids an additional grounding head.

The empirical evaluation spans three relevant benchmarks. Without zoom-in, GUI-AIMA achieves 45.2% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 56.9% on OSWorld-G, compared with reported GUI-Actor-3B results of 42.2% and 54.6%. These results support practical value beyond a single benchmark.

The controlled 45k-data ablations provide meaningful evidence for the design. On ScreenSpot-Pro, uniform anchor attention achieves 40.23%, versus 37.51% for vanilla attention and 35.99% for GUI-Actor; global top-1 weighting increases this to 42.13%, and weighted labels to 43.39%. These comparisons substantiate the core contribution independently of the headline zoom-in result.

The second-pass analysis reports both recovered and newly introduced errors, rather than only aggregate accuracy. Its substantial improvements on high-resolution screens demonstrate a useful application of the learned grounding maps.
weaknesses: The headline performance is not supported by matched inference-budget comparisons. Table 5 increases ScreenSpot-Pro accuracy from 47.06% to 58.57% through cropping and zooming, but equivalent refinement is not evaluated for GUI-Actor or other strong baselines. Moreover, 47.06% corresponds to the soft variant in Table 1, while the zoom-in row is labeled as ordinary GUI-AIMA. The manuscript should identify the actual starting model and distinguish gains from attention modeling from those obtainable through generic second-pass refinement.

Efficiency claims exceed the evidence. Figure 4 measures convergence against optimization steps, without wall-clock time, peak memory, or inference latency. Extracting multilayer attention and computing hidden-state similarities can introduce costs that parameter counts and step counts do not capture. Likewise, using 85k screenshots and 259k instructions is encouraging, but does not establish exceptional data efficiency without controlled data-scaling comparisons.

The soft-weighting formulation is incomplete as written. Equation (11) defines head weights as negative KL divergences, whereas Equation (4) uses weights to aggregate attention into a grounding distribution. A subsequent softmax or another positivity-preserving transformation is necessary but not explicitly specified. The construction of the general distribution from potentially signed cosine similarities also needs clarification. This matters because the soft variant supplies the strongest reported single-pass ScreenSpot-Pro result.

Claims about preserving general capabilities and identifying semantic attention heads are not directly validated. All model parameters are unfrozen, and no general vision-language retention evaluation is provided. Appendix A illustrates differences between hidden-state similarity and attention-based token scores, but does not establish that the selected heads are semantic or that avoiding interference explains the gains. These should be presented as hypotheses rather than demonstrated mechanisms.

Reproduction and comparison details remain insufficient: the image-resolution/token budget, exact attention-map-to-click decoding, relative weighting of attention and next-token losses, and baseline reproduction settings are not fully specified. Most main-table baselines are imported from other papers, and no run-to-run variability is reported. Consequently, small differences such as 90.8% versus 90.4% on ScreenSpot-v2 are less persuasive than the larger controlled ablation gains. Overall, those ablations support a slight preference for acceptance, but stronger efficiency evidence and a fully specified evaluation pipeline are needed.

strengths: As an Algorithms/General contribution, GUI-AIMA offers a useful refinement of coordinate-free GUI grounding: it supervises existing self-attention through an anchor token and adaptively weights attention heads without adding a separate grounding module. The distinction from TAG and GUI-Actor is clearly explained, and the Gaussian labeling component is appropriately attributed to GUI-G2.

The empirical results support the method's practical value across three benchmarks. Without zoom-in, GUI-AIMA achieves 45.2% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 56.9% on OSWorld-G, compared with the reported GUI-Actor-3B results of 42.2% and 54.6%. ScreenSpot-v2 performance is also competitive at 90.8%.

The controlled 45k-sample ablations provide meaningful evidence beyond comparisons with published results. On ScreenSpot-Pro, uniform anchor attention reaches 40.23%, versus 37.51% for vanilla attention grounding and 35.99% for GUI-Actor; global token selection and weighted labels further increase accuracy to 42.13% and 43.39%. These experiments support the individual design choices.

The crop-and-zoom analysis examines both recovered errors and lost correct predictions, providing useful evidence about the refinement stage's tradeoff. The reported two-pass results of 58.6% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 62.2% on OSWorld-G are substantial.

Training uses identified public data sources, with 259k instructions over approximately 85k screenshots and a single fine-tuning epoch. The combination of modest task-specific data requirements and competitive 3B performance makes the approach potentially useful for practical GUI agents.
weaknesses: The strongest results are not compared under matched inference budgets. Crop-and-zoom could also benefit competing grounding methods, but no corresponding baseline refinement is evaluated. Furthermore, Table 5 starts from 47.06%, matching the soft variant rather than the 45.2% default model, while Table 1 labels the zoom-in result as GUI-AIMA-3B without identifying the soft variant. This ambiguity prevents a clean attribution of the headline improvement.

Computational-efficiency claims exceed the available measurements. Figure 4 measures convergence against training steps, but the paper reports no wall-clock training cost, inference latency, or peak memory. Extracting attention and hidden states across layers, computing token similarities, and performing a second image pass can incur substantial costs; eliminating a grounding module does not establish an overall efficiency advantage.

The explanation that visual-sink selection identifies semantic heads and preserves general capabilities remains insufficiently demonstrated. There is no general-capability evaluation or direct controlled comparison against attention-derived token selection. Appendix A also claims that the embedding-based maximum favors the end-of-message token, whereas the displayed examples do not show this. The ablations support the heuristic's usefulness more convincingly than the proposed mechanism.

Several implementation details needed for reproduction are unclear: the precise conversion from a patch distribution to a click, image-resolution/token budgets, and the relative weighting of attention and next-token losses. Equation (11) gives negative KL divergence as an aggregation weight without specifying its conversion to nonnegative weights; it also leaves unclear how potentially negative cosine similarities become valid probability distributions. These omissions particularly affect reproduction of the soft variant.

Evidence for data efficiency and robustness is incomplete. Most main baselines use published results with different training data and settings, and the matched comparison is restricted to the smaller ablation dataset. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, so small differences such as the 0.4-point ScreenSpot-v2 gain over GUI-Actor should be interpreted cautiously. The demonstrated benefits support a slight preference for acceptance, but stronger efficiency measurements and clearer experimental specification would materially strengthen the case.

strengths: The paper makes a useful Algorithms/General contribution to GUI grounding: supervising native attention through an anchor token and selecting head weights using visual-sink query tokens. The combination is technically plausible and avoids a separate grounding module. Its distinction from TAG and GUI-Actor is reasonably clear.

The empirical results are strong across five benchmarks. Even without zoom-in, GUI-AIMA-3B achieves 53.8% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 62.8% on OSWorld-G; zoom-in increases these to 61.5% and 68.1%. Reporting both configurations helps distinguish model performance from inference-time refinement.

Controlled ablations provide substantive evidence beyond comparisons with published systems. In Table 5, anchored uniform aggregation improves ScreenSpot-Pro accuracy from 37.51% to 40.23%, visual-sink weighting raises it to 42.13%, and weighted labels yield 43.39%. Table 10 also compares against GUI-Actor using the same weighted labels, obtaining 49.78% versus 42.76%.

The paper includes useful practical and diagnostic evidence: selective attention extraction, training and inference timings, stop-gradient ablations, head-pruning experiments, and analysis of predictions corrected or lost through zoom-in. Table 8 reports reduced training cost relative to GUI-Actor, with modest single-pass inference overhead.
weaknesses: The strongest data-efficiency claims exceed the controlled evidence. Most headline baselines use different data mixtures, training procedures, and inference configurations. The matched GUI-Actor ablations are valuable, but there is no similarly controlled coordinate-generation baseline or data-scaling curve. Moreover, the lite-to-full comparison adds desktop-specific GroundCUA data, so it conflates data quantity with domain coverage.

Zoom-in contributes 7.7 percentage points on ScreenSpot-Pro and 5.3 points on OSWorld-G, yet the same crop-and-zoom procedure is not tested on competing methods. Such refinement is not exclusive to attention-based grounding. Matched two-pass comparisons and explicit two-pass latency would better establish the accuracy–cost advantage of the complete system.

Several details needed for reproduction are missing or inconsistent. The manuscript does not precisely specify how the patch distribution becomes a click point, the screenshot pixel/token budget, or the weighting between attention supervision and next-token loss. Training counts differ between 259k in Section 4.1 and 254k in Table 10, and between 250k additional GroundCUA instructions in Section 4.1 and 200k in Section 4.2. These appear correctable, but resolution and decoding choices are especially consequential for the reported gains.

The mechanistic interpretation is stronger than the supporting analysis. High total visual-attention mass need not imply target-specific localization, and similarity to the trained anchor's head-weight vector does not independently establish reliable grounding relevance. The pruning results support the heuristic's usefulness, but claims that it preserves pretrained capabilities or minimally perturbs other heads remain untested, particularly because all parameters are updated.

The smaller component gains lack uncertainty estimates or repeated runs, and the validation protocol for choosing token-selection settings and zoom factors is not stated. Some interpretations also overstate Table 5: global top-1 is not best on ScreenSpot-v2, and anchor-only weighting slightly improves ScreenSpot-Pro over uniform weighting. These issues warrant more calibrated conclusions but do not negate the larger controlled improvements.

strengths: The Algorithms/General contribution is technically meaningful: GUI-AIMA directly supervises native multimodal attention, combining an anchor token with adaptive head weighting to perform GUI grounding without a separate grounding head. The distinction from TAG and GUI-Actor is clearly explained.

The empirical results are strong across several benchmarks. Without zoom-in, the 3B model reaches 53.8% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 62.8% on OSWorld-G; zoom-in raises these to 61.5% and 68.1%. Thus, the contribution has value beyond its best two-pass result.

Controlled comparisons support an architectural benefit. In Table 10, with the same training set and weighted patch labels, GUI-AIMA-lite achieves 49.78% on ScreenSpot-Pro versus GUI-Actor's 42.76%, and 58.33% versus 55.14% on OSWorld-G. These comparisons are more persuasive than comparisons against differently trained published models.

The ablations examine anchor aggregation, token selection, head weighting, label construction, and gradient flow. The head-pruning analysis provides additional evidence that the learned weights identify useful grounding heads.

The implementation addresses attention-extraction overhead, and Table 8 reports lower training cost than GUI-Actor with similar single-pass inference time. The manuscript also explicitly identifies UI-Vision evaluation as in-domain.
weaknesses: The strongest data-efficiency claims exceed the controlled evidence. Most headline comparisons use published models with different data mixtures and training recipes. Adding GroundCUA changes both data quantity and domain coverage, so the resulting gains do not isolate sample efficiency. Matched-data coordinate-generation baselines and learning curves would strengthen this central claim.

Zoom-in contributes 7.7 percentage points on ScreenSpot-Pro, but the paper does not apply the same crop-and-zoom procedure to competing grounding methods. Consequently, this improvement cannot be attributed specifically to intrinsic attention grounding. Table 8 also does not clearly report the latency of the headline two-pass configuration.

Important reproduction details are missing or ambiguous: the exact conversion from patch probabilities to click coordinates, image-resolution/token budgets, the next-token prediction targets, and the weighting between language-model and attention losses. Training counts also conflict: 259k versus 254k for the lite setting, and 250k versus 200k added GroundCUA instructions.

The mechanistic interpretation is stronger than the evidence. Attention mass toward visual tokens does not itself establish target-specific grounding relevance, and similarity to the trained anchor in Appendix C does not establish stability during early training. Claims that the method preserves pretrained capabilities are unsupported by retention evaluations, particularly because all parameters are unfrozen.

Several component gains are modest and reported without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. The paper does not describe a separate validation protocol for choosing token-selection settings and zoom factors, although these choices are justified using benchmark results. This limits confidence in smaller improvements.

Originality lies primarily in the integration and adaptive weighting design: attention-based grounding, special-token localization, and distance-aware supervision have close precedents that the paper acknowledges. Overall, the substantial controlled gains support a slight preference for acceptance, but incomplete reproduction details and overextended efficiency claims prevent a stronger recommendation.

strengths: The paper offers a useful Algorithms/General contribution to GUI grounding: directly supervising native multimodal attention through an appended anchor token, with query-dependent head weighting. Although it builds on TAG and GUI-Actor, using intrinsic attention without an additional grounding module is a meaningful methodological distinction.

The empirical results are strong across five benchmarks. The 3B model achieves 53.8% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 62.8% on OSWorld-G with one-pass inference, increasing to 61.5% and 68.1% with zoom-in. Results on ScreenSpot-v2 and MMBench-GUI-L2 support usefulness beyond high-resolution desktop interfaces. The manuscript appropriately identifies UI-Vision results as in-domain.

Controlled ablations substantiate the main design choices. On the 45k training subset, anchored uniform aggregation improves ScreenSpot-Pro accuracy from 37.51% to 40.23%; visual-sink weighting raises it to 42.13%, and weighted labels to 43.39%. Table 10 provides stronger evidence at the larger training scale, including GUI-Actor with the same weighted labeling and a stop-gradient variant.

The implementation addresses the practical cost of extracting attention through selective row computation alongside FlashAttention. Table 8 reports comparable single-pass inference latency and reduced training cost relative to GUI-Actor, from approximately 260 to 192 A100 GPU-hours. The head-pruning analysis and crop/zoom error analysis provide useful supporting evidence.
weaknesses: The strongest headline results combine the grounding method with additional inference computation. Zoom-in accounts for 7.7 percentage points on ScreenSpot-Pro, but comparable crop-and-zoom experiments are not reported for GUI-Actor or a coordinate-generating baseline. Table 8 also does not separately quantify two-pass latency. Consequently, the results establish the effectiveness of the complete system more clearly than a distinctive advantage of coordinate-free grounding for refinement.

The broad data-efficiency claim is only partially isolated. Most main-table comparisons use published results with different training mixtures and budgets, and there is no coordinate-generating baseline trained on the same data and schedule. The matched GUI-Actor experiments are valuable, but comparable data-scaling curves would strengthen the claim that intrinsic attention supervision itself explains the efficiency.

Several details needed for reproduction remain unclear: the exact conversion from the patch distribution to a click point, image-resolution and visual-token limits, and the weighting of attention loss against next-token loss. The training description also needs reconciliation: the lite dataset is variously described as 259k and 254k elements, and the added GroundCUA subset as 250k and 200k instructions. These are correctable reporting issues, but they affect reconstruction of the experimental recipe.

The interpretation of visual-sink weighting is stronger than the evidence warrants. Head pruning supports its usefulness for grounding, but similarity to anchor-derived weights does not establish that the selected tokens reliably identify cross-modal correspondence. Claims that the method preserves pretrained capabilities or minimally perturbs unrelated heads are not tested on general vision-language tasks, despite all parameters being unfrozen.

Some component improvements are modest and vary by benchmark, without repeated-run uncertainty. For example, global top-1 selection is strongest on ScreenSpot-Pro, while layer-wise top-1 performs better on ScreenSpot-v2 in Table 5. The manuscript should clarify the validation protocol for choosing head-selection and zoom settings, especially because several alternatives are compared directly on the reported benchmarks.
